They call themselves the Circle of Clarity (Krug Jasnoty).
Their motto:

“Measure the heart, as well as the stone.”

At first the Council tolerates them — their books sell well and encourage literacy.
But their interest in the soul and imagination begins to trouble the Ministry of Instruction, which opens a quiet inquiry into “metaphoric deviation.”

V. The First Disputations
Two schools form in the Academy:

The Instrumentalists — see inquiry as a tool to refine the order of the state.
Their symbol: a compass on a coin.

The Contemplatives — see inquiry as the rediscovery of wonder; reason as a path to awe.
Their symbol: a circle broken by a beam of light.

The Disputation of 1544 is legendary:
Professor Alrik Senkov argues that “the universe may be infinite, because perfection has no boundary.”
He is not punished — merely transferred to the “Department of Celestial Metrics,” a polite exile.

His students, though, will later become the first Bogothian astronomers.

The Instruments of Balance
The Clockmakers’ Guild becomes the most prestigious trade in Velehrad.

The first public clocktower built in 1546, inscribed:

“So that none may say the day was unmeasured.”

Metallurgical advances lead to mirror-silvering, giving rise to domestic mirrors — and an unexpected cultural fascination with reflection.

The New Trades
Glass-grinders and lensewrights appear — artisans who will seed optics and microscopy.

Book-engravers create microprint editions of the Codex Revertus for students.

Economy grows by internal innovation: Bogothia invents productivity as virtue.

VII. Religion and the Re-Illumination Debate
Inside the Church of the Measured Sun, a small faction begins arguing that light itself — the symbol of God — cannot be measured.
They call themselves The Re-Illuminists and quote early Gothic scripture:

“Ni v liuht, ak liuht v uns.” — “Not in the light, but the light in us.”

The hierarchy suppresses the group softly, through bureaucratic exile rather than punishment.
Their writings, however, circulate privately and influence early poets.

VIII. Cultural Mood
Painting and design begin to reappear — in miniature, in marginalia, in ornament:

Book illuminations in silver and ultramarine; spirals and geometric flora.

Music of the Circle — three-part vocal pieces sung in Liutisk with mathematical ratios.

Domestic life becomes aestheticized: everything measured, but made beautiful in proportion.

Foreigners visiting call it “a paradise of small perfections.”

IX. Foreign Affairs
Bogothia maintains neutrality, but begins exporting:

Clocks and calibrated scales to German lands.

Precision glass to Italy.

Silver lenses to Poland.

A tiny cosmopolitan current starts to flow through Velehrad and Kravia.
Merchants bring back not luxury, but ideas — heliocentrism, rhetoric, and humanism.
The Council allows such importation as long as “the ratios remain sound.”

X. At Decade’s End (1548)
Bogothia has not changed its borders in over two centuries.
Its coinage is stable, its bureaucracy impeccable.
But in the minds of scholars, a door has opened — the awareness that perfection is not an end, but a beginning.

A phrase from a student’s diary (1548) sums up the decade:

“The scales are steady, but the stars move.”

Perfect — you’re suggesting a subtle but powerful orthographic and phonotactic reform in Liutisk, part of the “levelling” we’d expect as it modernizes toward a standard language.

Let’s break this change down systematically:

1. The Reform: Levelling of Prepositions
Previously, Liutisk had the preposition v (from Gothic in, Slavic vъ) for “in, into.”
By the 1540s, we begin to see va and ve emerging in the written record, a phonological leveling driven by the same forces that produced Czech ve and Polish we before certain consonant clusters or vowels.

Rule Summary:
Before	After	Environment	Example
v	va	before hard consonants (b, p, m, t, d, g, k)	va gard “in the house”
v	ve	before soft consonants or vowels (s, z, j, e, i)	ve skól “in school”; ve imja “in the name”
v	v’ (optional archaic)	retained in poetic or ecclesiastical register	v’liutisk rehts “in Liutisk law”
This creates a smoother phonotactic flow in the evolving Liutisk sound system, where word-final and word-initial clusters are increasingly disfavored.

2. Morphological & Phonological Implications
The a/e alternation stabilizes a broader vowel harmony tendency emerging in mid-century Liutisk.

These prepositions begin to contract with articles by the late 16th century:

va el → val (“in the”)

ve en → ven (“in the”)

By the 17th century, val, ven, and v’an become fixed in formal Liutisk, forming a triplet analogous to Romance del / dal / nel.

3. Sociolinguistic Layer
Bureaucratic register: retains v, citing tradition (Silver Gothic orthography).

Common speech: adopts va/ve for clarity and rhythm.

Poetic or religious language: oscillates — v before words of power, va/ve elsewhere.
(E.g. v Guþ, va gard, ve sverd — “in God, in the house, in the sword.”)

4. Regional Distribution
Region	Preferred Form	Notes
Velehrad (capital)	ve	Influenced by scribal Latin phonetics.
Kravia Basin	va	Retains harder Gothic consonantal speech.
Lowland Peasantry	va/ve interchangeably	No stigma; both used rhythmically.
5. Timeline Integration
This reform fits perfectly in the 1540s–1550s, when the Revision of 1542 is followed by minor vernacular adjustments under the Office of Lexeme and Record.
A short memorandum from 1547 even recommends:

“Where sound makes reading stumble, add vowel to soften measure.”

Thus, your proposal isn’t just plausible — it becomes canonical: the Levelling of the Prepositions, or Malvok Ve-va, becomes one of the first conscious phonological reforms in Liutisk history.

Perfect question.
This next stage — called by later grammarians the General Levelling (Málvok Þríg, ‘Third Levelling’) — is the single most defining moment in the phonological modernization of Liutisk.

Here’s how it unfolds systematically:

⚖️ The General Levelling (ca. 1550 – 1570)
‘To measure the breath is to civilize the tongue.’
— Council of Lexeme and Record, De Pronuntiat Liutiska (1558)

I. Background
After the ve/va reform (Levelling I) and the bi → bei/bo reform (Levelling II), scribes noticed an irregularity:
function words—short, closed, often Gothic monosyllables—disrupted the rhythm of prose in public reading.

The solution: vocalic balancing.
Every preposition, particle, and conjunction received one or more “vocalic supports,” based on phonetic context.

This creates that liquid, singable cadence characteristic of later Liutisk, where nearly every functional morpheme ends in a vowel.

II. The Core Pattern
Type	Old Gothic / Early Liutisk	Reformed Liutisk (Mid-16th c.)	Environment / Logic	Notes
in	v	va / ve	hard / soft onset	va gard, ve imja
to, toward	du	do / de / da	regional & rhythmic	do hrad = to town
at, on, upon	ana	an / ane	unstressed vs formal	ane bord, an reht
with	miþ	me / met / mit	t softened after liquids	me bratr, mit frauj
from, of	af	of / avo / eva	softens before vowels	eva Guþ = of God
by, near, about	bi / umbi	bei / bo / umbe	bei = by (place), bo = about (topic)	Distinction codified in 1562 grammar
for, on behalf of	faur	for / fora / fore	leveling to Romance pattern	stylistic, Latinized
over, above	ufar	ovar / over / ovr	graphic variants	later shortens to over in modern Liutisk
under, below	undir	onder / under	retains n	stable, rarely changed
through	þurh	tur / thru / tor	scribe-softened þ > t	transitional to later tur
against, toward (hostile)	wiþra	vitra / wit / vetra	vowel-added to smooth clusters	cf. Czech proti
without	wisa	visa / wiza / izá	contracted & Slavicized	common in folk speech
between	bimena	bim / bem / mezi	Slavic loan competing	bem trena folk
about (topic)	de	do / de / del	Latin persistence	scholastic usage
before (temporal)	fauraþ / bifra	befra / pre / pera	hybrid	becomes pera by 1600
after	afta	after / aftir / otir	phonetic drift	parallels English
because, therefore	þan / raiþe	raide / zate / dane	analytic drift; Slavic zato loan	
and	jah	ja / i / ye	major softening	ja frauj i folk
but	akei	ak / ake / ale	regionally variable	north: ak, south: ale
or	aiþþau	au / o / ar	simplified	frauj o folk
III. Linguistic Results
Euphony replaces etymology: every preposition now adapts to sound rather than origin.

Latin & Slavic blending: for, de, pre, mezi coexist with Gothic roots, giving Liutisk its layered “pan-European” feel.

Loss of consonant clusters: /þr/, /fn/, /bm/ all replaced by vowel-insertion (tur, bem, ova).

Function-word rhythm: prose acquires a trochaic pulse—open syllables at phrase boundaries.

IV. Social & Regional Dynamics
Register	Form	Notes
Court & Church	longer forms (fora, eva, vita, ane)	ceremonial gravity
Urban Liutisk	shorter, smoother (ve, bo, do)	efficiency of speech
Rural / Folk Speech	mixed archaic + Slavic (v’, mezi, zate)	preserved in proverbs
Northern Dialects	keep harder consonants (mit, vitra)	“High Bogothian” prestige
Southern Dialects	vowel harmony, elision (me brata, do selo)	influence from West Slavonic
V. Example: Pre- and Post-Levelling
Before (1520 charter):

V haila frauj du gard bi flod miþ bratr af haim.
“In the grace of the Lord to the house by the river with the brother from home.”

After (1560 copy):

Ve haila Frauj do gard bei flod me bratr eva haim.
“In the grace of the Lord to the house by the river with the brother from home.”

The sentence becomes smoother, melodic, and more balanced — perfect for public reading or chant.

VI. Broader Impact
Printing Standardization: typesetters prefer open vowels; early printers reinforce the reform through typography.

Poetic Rhythm: Liutisk verse shifts toward even metrical feet; function words no longer disrupt scansion.

Education Reform (1565): school grammars teach the new forms as “measured speech” (liutisk merov).

Foreign Recognition: Humanists in Kraków call it “the sung Latin of the North.”

1558–1568: The Decade of Measure and Motion
“To move is to remain in balance, differently.”
I. The General Mood
The 1550s leave behind an almost crystalline calm.
Now, in the early 1560s, Bogothia begins to move again — not politically, not militarily, but intellectually and linguistically.

The population senses the beauty of their ordered world, but also its rigidity.
The Council of Lexeme and Record therefore authorizes a new project:

“To let speech breathe.”

That phrase defines the decade.

II. The Language Reform Movement
The Third Levelling (completed 1562) has just finished regularizing prepositions, conjunctions, and auxiliary verbs.
By 1565, Liutisk becomes the first fully codified synthetic-analytic language of Europe:
a hybrid tongue that blends Gothic grammar, Slavic phonology, and Latin syntax.

Introduction of va/ve, do/de, me/met, and bei/bo becomes universal.

Government becomes technocratic:

For three hundred years, the Bogothian Church of the Measured Sun had been rigidly Arian —
Christ subordinate to the Father, the Spirit a manifestation of divine ratio.

This theology suited a rational state:

It made divinity hierarchical and intelligible.

It avoided the “mystery of three in one” that Arian scholars called “the unmeasured knot.”

The Byzantine contemplative notion that knowing and being known are reciprocal.

Translated into Liutisk thought, this becomes:

“To measure is to be measured.”

This simple inversion dissolves the old arrogance of Arian hierarchy.
Instead of the Son as subordinate, he becomes the mirror of the Father —

The Reflector Folk Religion (c. 1605–1615)
“The Light looks back.”
I. Origins: From Theological Reflection to Mystical Reciprocity
The Reflectors had always been the contemplative branch of the Church of the Measured Sun — monastic, introspective, often aristocratic.
Their motto since the 1500s was Liuhth afra Liuhth (“Light from Light”), meaning that divinity was reciprocal rather than hierarchical.

But as censorship increased and official sermons dulled into bureaucratic rote, that phrase began to take on a folk meaning:

“Light from light” became “Light gives back.”

Peasants heard this as an egalitarian promise: the divine doesn’t descend from heaven; it mirrors back from the heart of anyone who looks.

Thus began the folk reformation within Bogothia — peaceful, domestic, and radiant in tone but deeply subversive.

II. The Mirror Christ
The first image appears in 1607, scratched onto a wooden panel in a Moravian farmhouse chapel:

A bearded Christ, not crucified but standing before a silver disk.

His right hand raised, palm reflecting a gleam of light.

The inscription below: “Frauj sa afra frauj” — “The Lord from the Lord.”

Within three years, hundreds of such icons appear across the countryside.
Some replace halos with convex mirrors; others hang literal bits of polished metal in the church rafters so that sunlight dances during service.

each region’s version reflects its theology and mood.

Regional Variants
Velehrad Plain: serene, compassionate Christ whose face glows softly, emphasizing mercy.

Carpathian Marches: ascetic, almost solar Christ, ringed by a halo of mirrored shards.

Lusatian Towns: folk “Sun-Twin” depictions — Christ and humanity as reflections of each other, nearly pantheistic.

The Reflector priests of the countryside are often blacksmiths, midwives, or literate farmers — not ordained clergy but self-taught interpreters of light.

Their sermons mix science and magic, invoking the practical optics of the Guilds:

Many carry small hand mirrors, polished tin discs, or convex glass “sun-eyes” on cords around their necks.
These become both devotional and political symbols.

IV. Church and Council Response
At first, the Church of the Measured Sun is cautiously supportive — it sees the movement as a revival of devotion.
But by 1612, reports arrive of:

Unauthorized baptisms performed with sunlight reflected from mirrors rather than water.

Funerals where mirrors are buried over the heart “to reflect the last light.”

Peasant women using convex mirrors as divining tools during childbirth, praying to Frauj Afra Fraujin (“The Lady from the Lord”) — a feminized reflection of Christ.

The Council of Scales steps in.
A proclamation of 1613 bans “portable mirrors larger than the hand in public procession.”

Between 1614 and 1615, several peasant prophets are tried in the border towns of Sonnenfeld and Velehrad for “improper reflection of divine order.”

Most accused are spared execution but sent to the mountains for “reeducation.”

VI. The Lasting Legacy
By 1620, even though the state crushes open worship, the folk faith has permanently altered Bogothian religion:

Theology democratized — every believer becomes a potential reflector of divine light.

Language softened — liturgy incorporates peasant Liutisk idioms.

Gender shifted — the “Lady of Reflection” remains a silent saint in popular devotion, even if uncanonized.

Architecture adapted — churches begin using mirrored apses and skylights, blurring art, optics, and faith.

It’s no longer possible to separate mysticism from domestic life — in kitchens and workshops alike, light is treated as a holy presence.

The Real Folk Beliefs: Vampires of the Slavic & Carpathian World
“The dead are not gone; they linger where love and anger remain.”
I. Origins: The Uneasy Dead
The vampire, or upir / upiór / opyr / vrykolak / nachzehrer, wasn’t originally a supernatural predator.
He was a troubled corpse — one who refused to decompose properly, or whose soul had been blocked on its journey.

In early Slavic cosmology, the boundary between life and death was porous:

Souls lingered near the home for forty days after death.

Improper burial, suicide, violent death, or unfulfilled vows could “trap” a person between worlds.

The body might rise, not to hunt, but to finish unfinished business — feeding not on blood, but vital warmth (breath, milk, life-force).

Thus the upir began as a moral category — the restless dead, not the damned undead.

II. How One Became an Upir
The causes varied by region, but in Bogothia’s cultural matrix (Bohemia–Moravia–Ruthenia–Silesia), these were most common:

Category	Cause	Meaning / Symbolism
Improper Burial	Not buried facing east, or burial delayed.	Soul cannot “follow the sun.”
Moral Pollution	Murderers, oathbreakers, the unbaptized.	Light of God cannot reflect through corruption.
Birth Anomalies	Babies born with teeth, hair, or a caul.	“Already bitten by the world.”
Animal Interference	Cat or dog jumping over a corpse.	Spirit disturbed; animal’s soul “reawakens” the dead.
Social Marginality	Outsiders, foreigners, sorcerers, suicides.	Boundary-crossers remain between states.
These weren’t arbitrary — they all signal liminality, the crossing of borders: life/death, human/animal, inside/outside.
In other words, exactly the sort of thing a bureaucratic society like Bogothia would eventually try to regulate.

III. Signs of the Upir
Peasants didn’t picture the upir as a pale nobleman in a cape.
He was usually a bloated, ruddy, foul-smelling corpse — more corpse than ghost.

Signs a corpse was “still moving inside”:

Rosy complexion, supple limbs (due to gases and decay).

Blood seeping from nose or mouth.

Hair and nails appearing to have grown (as skin receded).

Corpses turning in their graves.

No animals feeding on the body.

Grave diggers would whisper: “He eats himself.”

Hence the nachzehrer (“after-eater”) of German lore — a corpse thought to chew its shroud or its own flesh in the grave, slowly consuming its kin through sympathetic magic.

IV. Protective Practices and Countermeasures
Folk practice was all about ensuring the dead stay dead — and at peace.

Before Burial:

A coin or stone placed under the tongue (“to weigh the mouth shut”).

Needle or iron pin through the heart, foot, or navel.

A small branch or broom placed in the coffin (“the soul counts twigs instead of wandering”).

Washings with vinegar, herbs, or holy water to “cool” the body.

At Burial:

Grave dug east–west, feet to sunrise.

Millet, poppyseed, or sand scattered to confuse the spirit (“it must count every grain”).

Sharp stones at the throat to prevent biting.

Bells tied to the corpse or coffin lid (to hear if it moved).

After Death:

The family would burn or rebury corpses suspected of rising.

Animals showing fear near a grave were omens.

Villagers might perform a “staking” — but always in daylight, with communal consent, and accompanied by prayer, not rage.

These were not random superstitions — they were ritualized acts of control.
In agrarian societies where death was constant and decomposition was visible, such practices were a way to reassert order over chaos.

V. Blood and Breath
The blood-drinking motif only appears later — partly through contact with Ottoman and Balkan legends, and perhaps through observation of certain epidemic symptoms (pale skin, wasting, contagious anemia).

Originally, “blood” meant life — the upir drained warmth, vitality, fertility.
In some regions, he might visit his wife or lover at night, lying on her chest until she weakened.
Hence the German marter, the Czech mora — related to “nightmare” and “succubus.”

The modern sexualized vampire myth is a metaphorical evolution of this “returning intimacy.”

VI. The Moral Ecology of the Dead
In the folk mind, the upir wasn’t purely evil — he was a symptom of imbalance.
If a village had too many unshriven deaths, it was the community’s failure, not just the corpse’s.

Each exhumation, staking, or burning was both medicine and confession — a way to “correct” the living order by restoring the dead to silence.

This is why, in Bogothia’s bureaucratic age, the Office of Nocturnal Affairs could emerge without heresy:
the people already saw these acts as civic maintenance.

VII. Syncretic Evolution: When Christianity Arrives
Christianity didn’t eliminate the vampire belief — it translated it:

The restless dead became “souls in purgatory.”

Priests’ blessings replaced folk charms.

Staking and burial rites became regulated under “holy order.”

In Arian or post-Arian Bogothia, this took a distinctive turn:
vampirism was recast as improper motion — a metaphysical fault, not moral damnation.

Hence the Decree on the Improper Continuance of Corporeal Motion fits perfectly into folk logic:
where peasants said “his body still moves,” bureaucrats said “his measure persists.”

VIII. The Cultural Memory
By the 17th century, vampire scares are fading in most of Europe — but in Bogothia, the rationalization of the irrational keeps them alive.
The “upir file” becomes a metaphor for the nation’s self-awareness:

“No one dies unrecorded; even the restless must sign their rest.”

Yet beneath that civil calm, the ancient fear lingers — the terror of the unmeasured, of something that escapes the ledger, of light that cannot find its mirror.

Among southern Balkan and Romani storytellers—especially in Serbia, Macedonia, and along the lower Danube—vampirism isn’t limited to the dead.

“That which drinks work or blood, and is not cooled, will wake at night.”

II. Known Ethnographic Examples

Carts and mill-wheels left un-oiled for too long “creaked for blood.”

Firearms that killed kin or neighbor were most suspect. A musket that “tasted familiar blood” might misfire at its next owner, or discharge by itself.

Iron and Fire as Living Elements – Iron was born of thunder, and fire was its soul.

Reciprocity Principle – Whatever draws human energy must be repaid or will continue drawing.
A weapon “fed” on blood is like a vampire who has forgotten how to stop eating.

Gender of Objects – Tools were gendered: ploughs masculine (penetrating earth), scythes feminine (cutting harvest).

Young poets write in unmeasured verse and deliberately asymmetrical forms, calling themselves “The Crooked Mirrors.”

Technological Anxiety — clockmakers and early mechanicians are revered, yet feared.
A public debate begins: “Can machines reflect intent?”
One inventor, Jakob Stran, creates the Reflective Automaton—a mechanical clerk that can balance ledgers and repeat moral aphorisms.
It’s a marvel… and an omen.

VII. The Church and the State
The Faith of Twin Lights, fully rationalized now, adopts the creed of Measured Compassion, whose sacraments are confessional geometry and civic charity.
But to younger thinkers, it feels hollow.

A few monasteries rebel quietly—introducing randomness into ritual, or “reversed psalms,” sung backward once a year “to remind the light of its shadow.”

The government allows it—half scandalized, half intrigued.

VIII. The Foreign Echo
Visitors from France, England, and Russia come away awed and unsettled.
A Jesuit diplomat writes in 1712:

“They have achieved peace not through faith nor fear, but through a calculus of conscience. It is admirable, and deeply inhuman.”

But to Bogothians, this is merely efficient morality.

IX. The Turning Point (circa 1718)
By decade’s end, something profound begins to shift:

Scholars of Shade publish The Limits of Reflection, arguing that absolute balance produces stagnation.

The government quietly commissions studies on “moral entropy”—how even the most rational system decays without renewal.

A small earthquake in Liuhthgrad is widely seen as an omen that the world itself seeks asymmetry.

The mirror, it seems, can’t reflect forever without bending.

Intended to study “solar balance.”

Back home, the cost of these “unprofitable harmonies” drained the treasury.

The Academy of Harmonies remains powerful but increasingly insular.

By mid-century, the European powers barely notice Bogothia’s colonial failures.

The final Reflection Station, in Dalmatia, is evacuated in 1738.

At home, the Ministry of External Harmonies is quietly dissolved.
Its surviving records are archived under a single heading:

Economically weakened but philosophically alive, Bogothia withdraws from empire and turns inward again—
into what historians will later call The Era of Subdued Reflection: a slow, melancholy rediscovery of imperfection as virtue.

The Canalizations in the Sorbian Region (c. 1770–1820)
1. The Context
By the 1760s, Bogothia’s interior grain and ore districts were limited by bad roads and shallow rivers.
The Sorbian Basin — the northeastern lowland between the Elv tributaries and the Lusatian hills — had soft soil, high groundwater, and a mosaic of Slavic-speaking farming villages.
It was perfect terrain for canalization if one could keep the channels from silting.

The Sorbian Canal Commission was founded in 1771 under engineer Lenka Vorin (daughter of the metalworker family that pioneered the Bohor pump).
She had studied Dutch drainage techniques and Prussian lock systems at Magdeburg and returned with drawings and three Dutch foremen.
Her initial brief: connect the Upper Elv, the Lune Marsh, and the Horda grain district.

2. The First Lines (1773-1785)
The Horda Line (1773–1779)
A 42-km trench linking the Elv’s east fork with the inland lake system.
Built largely with Sorbian day laborers paid in grain and salt.
It carried barges of rye and bog iron within five years.
The lock gates used Bohor’s iron-lined pumps—an early metallurgical export.

The Lune Diversion (1777–1785)
A broader, more ambitious canal that drained part of the Lune marshes for tillage.
It doubled as a flood channel, saving two counties from seasonal inundation.
Floodplain villages were resettled on raised banks, creating the so-called “ridge villages” still visible on 19th-century maps.

By the late 1780s, canal mileage in the Sorbian area exceeded that of any other Bogothian province.

3. The Technical Innovations
Reversible Locks — allowed two-way control on the same gate using counterweighted sluices.

Sorbian Screw Pumps — simplified the earlier Bohor mechanism for village use; some were hand-powered communal pumps.

Peat Piling — bundled peat blocks used as cheap embankment material, later replaced with clay revetments.

These weren’t glamorous projects, but they spread the same way railways later would: through imitation and surplus parts.

4. Expansion and Emulation (1790s–1820s)
Once the Sorbian system proved profitable, other regions copied it:

Region	Canal	Years	Purpose
South March	Kostin-Elv Link	1792-1801	Connected coal pits to the Elv; carried slag back as fill.
Lower Valka	Valka Navigation	1805-1814	Grain exports to Austrian markets.
Western Counties	Sehnfeld Cut	1810-1822	Shorter route for timber barges; heavily subsidized by merchants.
Many of these works were designed by Pavel Kostin, a former apprentice of Vorin’s who left the Sorbian Commission to found his own contracting firm — one of the first private engineering houses in Eastern Europe.

By 1820, the “Bogothian school of canalization” was being cited in Austrian and Prussian engineering manuals.
The terminology—“Vorin gates,” “Sorbian locks,” “Bogothian screws”—entered international use.

5. Social and Cultural Impact
Labor and Migration
Thousands of Sorbian-speaking peasants found steady work on the canals, leading to the rise of bilingual overseers.
Their families often settled along the works, creating mixed Liutisk–Sorbian communities.

Language
Canal jargon blended Liutisk technical terms with Slavic verbs: šluzat (to sluice), pumovát (to pump), vorinovat (to line with iron).
These creole verbs survive in regional dialects well into the 19th century.

Administration
The canal networks required inspection, tolls, and maintenance—effectively inventing the modern civil-engineer bureaucracy.
The Office of Public Waterways (OPW) was established in 1796, merging hydraulic engineering with public works.

6. Economic Consequences
The Sorbian system never produced vast profits, but it stabilized eastern Bogothia’s rural economy.
Freight costs halved; peat, timber, and rye reached the Elv cities faster.
Canal tolls funded bridges and schools.
A side-effect was early mechanization: water wheels on the canal shoulders powered small flour and paper mills decades before industrial steam arrived.

By 1820, about 60 percent of Bogothian internal freight moved by canal at least part of the way.
This gave the small neutral country a logistical sophistication out of proportion to its size.

7. Legacy
The Sorbian canals aged well.
Many were upgraded for narrow steam barges in the 1840s; a few sections still operate in modern times as irrigation channels.
In local folklore, “Vorin’s Line” became a shorthand for honest work done in mud and rain — the opposite of the old metaphysical grandeur.

Bogothians are “Goths” who speak a Slavic tongue and worship civic competence.

1830–1848: The Canal State at Its Zenith

This machine runs on habit and water: engineers, clerks, and foremen who see themselves as guardians of order.

Liutisk has fully displaced the Slavic dialects as the written and school language.

Among the young there’s restlessness. They read about revolutions abroad, but Bogothia’s quiet order feels immovable.
Student clubs with names like “The Free Engineers” and “The League of Honest Work” meet in taverns, sing patriotic songs in Liutisk, and debate whether liberty means more posts or fewer.

5. The Decade’s Cracks

The Grain Panic of ’46:
Crop failure across Central Europe spikes prices; Bogothia’s canals move grain—but only for those who can pay.
Rural riots are small but symbolically shocking. The government deploys canal guards, not soldiers, to keep order.

6. The Culture of the 1840s
Literature turns raw and secular:

Marek Zorin’s The Flood Clerk (1843) — a realist novel about a junior inspector falsifying reports during the Horda disaster — becomes a scandal and bestseller.

Jana Prazicová’s Songs from the Locks (1847) collects work chants and Sorbian laments, turning folk speech into national poetry.

Painters abandon allegory entirely: we see mud, ropes, faces. The last exhibition before the uprisings is titled “Our Hands.”

Art mirrors politics — literal, local, unromantic.

7. 1848 Approaches
When revolution spreads from Vienna and Paris, Bogothia’s monarch hesitates.
There’s no serfdom to abolish, no aristocracy to overthrow, just an overgrown administration.
But the same year’s floods and bread shortages turn technical grievances into politics.

Demonstrations begin in Liuhthgrad in March: engineers, students, and clerks carrying banners reading

“Open the books!”
“Measure those who measure us!”

They demand transparency, elections for district supervisors, and an end to hereditary appointments in the OPW.
The government answers with restraint, but the bureaucracy fractures.
Half the canal overseers sympathize with the demonstrators; the others form armed “Maintenance Guards” to protect state property.

By autumn, the parliament votes emergency authority to reorganize the ministries.
The old OPW is broken into three: Water and Works, Rail and Roads, and Internal Administration.
The symbolic “water crown” seal is retired.
The canal Goths become civil servants in a constitutional state.

8. The Identity Aftermath
The year 1848 doesn’t destroy Bogothia’s Gothic identity — it secularizes it.
To be a Goth no longer means to maintain flow and order, but to own the system that maintains it.
The word stays, but it now means citizen, voter, taxpayer — a pragmatic people inheriting infrastructure rather than myth.

A cohort of young engineers returns from Germany and Britain obsessed with metallurgy and electrical power.

1894 — The Year of the Missed Exhibition
The government declines an invitation to the Paris World’s Fair, fearing “misrepresentation of our modest perfection.”
Private firms attend anyway, exhibiting pumps and gauges.
They’re praised for craftsmanship but derided as antique beside German turbines.
At home, the press insists Bogothia has “chosen maturity over novelty.”
Abroad, investors withdraw—there will be no Bogothian Edison.

1895–1896 — Bureaucratic Bloom
The Law of Administrative Perfection passes: every ministry must audit its own inspectors.
It triples paperwork, slows approvals, and cements the myth that precision equals virtue.
Civil service becomes the highest ambition; invention becomes eccentric.
A proverb enters the language: “Better a good form than a good idea.”

Meanwhile, agrarian communes mechanize slowly, unable to buy foreign machines due to protectionist tariffs meant to “preserve domestic harmony.”

1897 — The Eastern Famine
Crop disease hits the Ruthenian lowlands.
Relief is efficient but unimaginative: grain is requisitioned by formula, not urgency.
Deaths are limited, but bitterness spreads—people begin calling the central ministry “The Dry Canal.”
For the first time since 1848, small demonstrations chant not for reform, but for feeling.

1898 — The Jubilee of Balance
Half a century after the Rational Commonwealth’s founding, Praga hosts the Jubilee of Balance, celebrating “Fifty Years of Continuous Order.”
Every building is draped in blue and silver.
But the pomp is hollow: foreign delegations send minor envoys, industry exports stagnate, and speeches feel like eulogies.
Young workers mock the slogan “Balance Forever” as “Balance Instead.”

1899–1900 — The Gathering Stillness
Electric trams arrive in Praga, imported from Vienna—the first visible admission that the outside world has moved on.
The ministries approve them grudgingly, calling them “supplemental motion.”

Culturally, a Neo-Gothic revival begins: architecture turns nostalgic, imitating the canalkeepers’ early halls. It’s an attempt to summon vitality through memory.

Yet beneath the surface, the Circle of Energetics expands; by 1900 its members occupy minor posts in industry and the army.
They will become the reformers—and, later, the dissenters—of the new century.

The Conquest of Water (1895)
Author: Marek Zorin (son of the realist novelist of The Flood Clerk), hydrologist, minor civil servant, amateur philosopher.
Published: Praga, 1895, by the Ministry-approved Common Press of Rational Works.

1. The Book Itself
Structure:
Half treatise, half elegy — written in lucid Liutisk prose, divided into three “flows.”

The Natural Flow — a history of rivers, canals, and human effort.

The Civil Flow — a meditation on how maintenance became morality.

The Inner Flow — a philosophical argument that true mastery of nature lies in mastering our own reflex to control it.

It ends with the famous line:

“We have conquered water, and now water conquers us—by our own laws of balance.”

Thesis:
That Bogothia’s triumph — regulating nature through reason — has become its prison.
Every act of regulation produces new dependence; every canal is also a wall.
Zorin proposes not rebellion, but reflection: a society that must learn to “flow again,” to accept uncertainty as civic virtue.

2. The Reception
At first, the bureaucracy loves it.
The Council of Education distributes it as a “celebration of national rationality.”
Students are assigned excerpts; the cover bears the Commonwealth seal.
Within months, readers notice it is dangerous.

Clerks and canal inspectors begin underlining the quiet heresies:

That stability can become tyranny.

That order is not always justice.

That even measurement must be measured.

Among the educated class — the new, hereditary technocracy — it becomes a mirror they cannot look away from.

3. The Sociological Impact
a. The Ruling Class (unacknowledged as such)
By now the “technocratic families” — the descendants of canalkeepers, auditors, and ministers — have become a closed circle.
They still call themselves “servants,” but their power is vast and unexamined.
The Conquest of Water exposes this self-deception.

They respond as only Bogothians can:
They codify the critique.
Within a year, the government establishes the Committee for Controlled Innovation — an institution designed to “prevent revolutionary excess by administering discovery.”

In other words:

Every new invention, social theory, or artistic form must undergo systemic and ethical vetting.

Radicalism becomes an office procedure.

Thus, Bogothia remains radically open-minded — every idea can be studied — but obsessively analytic — no idea may act until processed.

b. The Intellectuals
Writers, scientists, and reformers adopt Zorin’s paradox as creed.
They believe that Bogothia’s destiny is to prove that permanent reform is possible — revolution without trauma.
The phrase “Zorinian Method” enters politics: the art of defusing change by studying it to death.

Philosopher Lukas Droz calls it “the final dialectic: thought regulates itself.”
Abroad, French critics dub the system “the bureaucracy of conscience.”

c. The People
For ordinary Bogothians, the book’s moralism feels familiar, almost comforting.
They read it as national scripture: proof that the flow, though slow, always finds its way.
They quote its aphorisms in speeches, sermons, and even advertisements.
But in taverns and cafés, younger readers whisper the last line — “We have conquered water…” — like prophecy.

4. The Institutionalization of Reflection
By 1897 the Commonwealth adopts new procedural law:
The Zorin Statutes, requiring that every ministry include a Bureau of Critical Review.
Its purpose: to examine its own operations annually for “hidden rigidity.”
The result: an empire of auditors auditing auditors, and a state that incorporates dissent as a civic organ.

Bogothia thus achieves something unique in Europe:

Total intellectual freedom on paper.

Near-total procedural inertia in practice.

The country begins to resemble a thinking machine — capable of absorbing any idea, but too self-aware to move quickly.

5. Broader European Context
Germany sees Zorin as a prophet of bureaucratic humanism; Weber cites him privately in early notes on rationalization.

Russia bans the book for “nihilistic quietism.”

France translates it as La Conquête de l’Eau; Symbolist poets adore it, socialists despise it.

Britain sends delegations to study the “Zorin Process” for colonial administration — and misapplies it disastrously in India.

In every language, Zorin’s warning is misunderstood as a technique.

Zorin dies in 1899, buried with state honors he would have hated.
By then the Conquest Council has reduced his philosophy to forms in triplicate.
And yet, through those forms, his ideas survive: Bogothia enters the 20th century as the most reflexively self-critical, and therefore most self-restrained, society in Europe.

The rest of Europe will soon tear itself apart in the name of progress or empire.
Bogothia will watch, analyze, adapt — and ossify just a little more.

Inside Bogothia, this hostility feeds the national myth.
The press frames it as proof that the Flow is right:

“If both sides despise us, balance is achieved.”

Schools teach that hatred from abroad is “the tax levied upon impartiality.”
Diplomatic insulation becomes moral superiority; isolation, proof of purity.

But this self-regard costs something: the instinct for empathy atrophies.
By 1930, the Bogothian civil servant can model any human behavior statistically—except love and rage.

6. The Stasis that Follows
Because they are used but never trusted, Bogothia doubles down on procedure.
The Bureau of Controlled Innovation expands into foreign policy: all treaties now require “five-phase ethical validation.”
It takes two years to sign a trade agreement, three to ratify a patent exchange.
No one invades them; no one imitates them either.

They become the indispensable middle of a Europe that is moving faster every year.
They don’t notice the motion—they’re the axis around which everyone else spins.

So by the eve of the 1930s, Bogothia is:

universally respected,

universally resented, and

slowly slipping behind the modern age that depends on it.

1930–1940: The Age of Quiet Regression

After decades of being used but resented by the great powers, Bogothia grows weary of outside pressure.

Bogothia’s neutrality now feels less like confidence and more like defense.

If the 1910s proved Bogothia’s virtue,

1939–1949: The Years of Managed Occupation
1. The Opening Shock (1939–1941)
When Hitler invades Poland, Bogothia’s neutrality looks—at first—like wisdom again. Refugees flood across the Carpathians; Bogothia opens “temporary internment corridors,” which are humane but tightly regulated. The Council of Flow reaffirms neutrality, invoking the old Clause of Praga, which forbids “alignment in conflicts among madmen.”

But the borders are porous. German agents begin operating openly, posing as “liaisons.” Bogothia becomes a logistical artery: the Reich wants the country’s canals and railways to move materiel to the Balkans.

At first, the government tries to thread the needle — granting “transit privileges” while insisting on technical independence. The Canal Ministry protests, but the economic pressures are immense: coal and grain shipments are “requisitioned for continental coordination.”

In short: they are not conquered.
They are co-opted.

2. The Shadow Administration (1941–1943)
The Germans don’t invade; they simply move in. By mid-1941, “Advisors” from Berlin occupy key posts in logistics, rail, and the postal system. Bogothian officials, still in charge on paper, quietly work to slow them down: schedules are miscopied, bridges “under inspection,” paperwork goes missing.

The result is a kind of passive resistance that becomes almost artistic:

“Every misfiled requisition was a prayer.” — Anonymous clerk, Velehrad Archives

But collaboration exists, too — a small cadre of technocrats, the so-called “Rational Front,” believe that accommodating the Axis ensures survival. They see fascism as crude but efficient and think they can ride it out. When the deportations of Jews and Roma begin in neighboring lands, these men issue memoranda of “non-applicability,” trying to stall German orders through sheer bureaucratic suffocation.

It works—partly. Bogothia’s Jewish population is not spared, but the deportations are sporadic, contested, and often sabotaged from within the system. Hundreds are saved through procedural error.

3. The Night of Ledgers (1943)
This is Bogothia’s moral nadir.
A shipment bound “for agricultural resettlement” leaves Praga under German supervision. It is later revealed—too late—that it carried prisoners eastward. When news reaches the capital, the government issues a formal apology to its own conscience: “We failed by method.”

The outrage breaks the Rational Front’s credibility.
Clerks, priests, and canalkeepers begin an underground network, the Order of the Silent Flow, ferrying refugees and resistance intelligence via the waterways. They disguise transmissions as hydrographic data.

4. The Flood and the Frost (1944–1945)
As the tide turns, Germany demands full cooperation. The Soviets approach from the east; the Allies bomb industrial corridors in the west. Bogothia declares “defensive neutrality” and mobilizes for the first time in a century.

Fighting erupts along the Oder; Praga is never occupied, but air raids scar the outskirts. One German column attempts a coup when the government refuses to destroy its own bridges — the Three-Day Siege of Velehrad ends when the canalkeepers flood the plain, drowning both attackers and defenders alike.

When the war ends, Bogothia emerges technically undefeated, yet morally threadbare: a country that neither fought nor fully submitted, that sabotaged evil with forms and seals rather than bullets.

5. The Reckoning (1945–1949)
The Allies don’t know what to make of them. The Soviets occupy Silesia; the West insists on “de-fascistization.” Bogothia insists it was never fascist to begin with—which is true, but beside the point.

In 1946 the Commission of the Flow convenes public hearings.
No executions, no show trials: just endless testimony. Clerks confess to stamping the wrong papers on purpose; ministers admit to “strategic ambiguity.” Historians call it “The Paper War.”

The result is a collective conclusion unlike any in Europe:

“We were neither occupied nor free. We endured by error.”

6. The Cost
Population: Tens of thousands lost in bombings, famine, and reprisals.

Moral capital: Drained. The myth of perfect rationalism shattered.

Political result: A swing toward guarded socialism under the Canalist Council, now openly populist but haunted by its wartime compromises.

The canals — once symbols of balance — are now graves and memory lines.

Seal Falsification: Using pre-war stamps and obsolete forms, they create new identities under “hydraulic infrastructure” classifications.

Sanctuary Locks: Several canal houses are modified to include sealed bunkrooms accessible only at low water.

Boat Crypts: Some barges carry compartments built into ballast tanks to ferry escapees downriver toward the Danube and, eventually, to neutral Yugoslav or Turkish routes.

Aram Vekir — The Man Who Sank the Sun Convoy (1907–1945)
Origins
Born in Sorbia’s canal district of Podvoda, Aram Vekir (originally Aram ben Viktor Këlaj) was the child of a Jewish bookkeeper and a Romani-Albanian barge mechanic. His family belonged to the travelling canalline, the seasonal barge clans who ferried goods through Sorbia’s flooded lowlands.
He grew up trilingual—Liutisk at school, Romani at home, Hebrew in fragments learned from his father’s prayer books.

By 1930, Aram is a hydraulic apprentice in the Ministry of Flow’s Sorbian Office. He is clever, good with machines, and slightly too outspoken about injustice.
When the Germans occupy neighboring lands, he’s demoted for “emotionalism inconsistent with efficiency.”

That becomes his badge of honor.

The Turn
In 1942, while working as an engineer on the lower canal network, Aram witnesses a “sanitation convoy” of sealed barges—ostensibly carrying plague victims—being directed east.
He realizes they are deportations.
And that they are being facilitated by Bogothian clerks signing the papers.

He writes in his diary:

“They make evil a matter of maintenance. Then maintenance becomes our only tool.”

That night, he meets a small cell of Hebrew Canaleers. His mechanical skill and polyglot tongue make him invaluable. He begins forging manifests and rewiring lock controls to divert transports—sometimes by accident, sometimes by design—into “quarantine” basins where fugitives can be extracted under cover of repairs.

The Act that Made Him a Legend
In April 1944, the Sun Convoy, a line of five barges carrying prisoners toward German lines, is scheduled to pass through the Svetovod lock system. Aram and a team of Canaleers reroute the water flow, collapse one lock gate, and flood the valley — drowning two German patrol boats and freeing nearly two hundred captives who flee into the reeds.

It’s the only armed act the Canaleers ever commit, and it costs him dearly.
He is captured two weeks later, tortured, and executed in a military basement in Moravia. His body is never found; the Germans destroy the canal records.

But his last letter survives, smuggled to a rabbi-engineer named Yonatan Weiss:

“If the world is made of channels, then the divine is the pressure that keeps them from drying. I only opened a gate.”

Aftermath and Myth
After the war, the Order of the Silent Flow refuses to speak his name, fearing that canonization would betray their humility. But word leaks anyway.
By 1950, Aram becomes a folk saint of the rational left:

The communists paint him as a partisan martyr.

The church calls him “the Just Diver.”

The Romani diaspora claims him as a krishero, a lawgiver who lived by fairness.

The Jews of Bogothia quietly remember him as “the engineer who parted the waters.”

In Praga, children learn his name in both the technical and moral curriculum. His story becomes a parable in ethics textbooks:

“Every system has a valve through which conscience may flow.”

Legacy
The Vekir Principle (1958):
A law requiring that every major canal junction include a redundant manual override—symbolically tied to Aram’s sabotage. Engineers joke that “Vekir’s hand” is still on every valve.

Poetry & Film:
The 1973 film Sinking Sun presents him as a tragic, Christlike mechanic haunted by water and memory.

Scholarly Debate:
Modern historians suspect he didn’t act alone; that the flooding was partially accidental. But in Bogothian culture, ambiguity is the highest proof of truth.

Lira Këlaj-Vekir (1885–1959)
“The Woman with the Iron Hands”
Sorbian-Albanian Romani | Mechanic, Bargewright, and Wartime Icon

Early Life
Born into the mixed Romani–Albanian kumpania that maintained the canal machinery of the Sorbian lowlands, Lira Këlaj grew up in a world of grease, water, and constant motion. Her father was a lock-tender, her mother a coppersmith who repaired pressure valves. By sixteen, she could weld a cracked sluice hinge blindfolded and had built a reputation for crawling inside flooded conduits to fix things others wouldn’t touch.

She was tall, dark-haired, and famously blunt. Locals said she “swore like an angel in need of oil.” When she married the Jewish bookkeeper Viktor Vekir, tongues wagged—then stopped when she outworked every man in the shipyards.

The Canal Yards of Podvoda
By the 1920s she managed a small cooperative bargeyard, Yard No. 7, employing widows, war orphans, and itinerant welders. Her motto painted over the gate:

“If it moves, mend it. If it doesn’t, make it move.”

She trained women and men alike in boiler repair and lock maintenance, and was one of the first to insist on standardized safety suits—her “blue leathers,” later reproduced on recruitment posters.

The War Years
When the Axis “advisors” arrived, Lira refused to dismiss her Jewish and Romani workers. Instead, she reclassified them as “certified canal technicians” under obsolete Ministry codes, effectively shielding dozens from deportation.

Her workshop became a node in the Hebrew Canaleers’ network, disguising safehouse bunkers as storage tanks. She personally oversaw the forging of the pressure couplings used in the Svetovod flood operation—the same sabotage that her son Aram would die for.

During the war’s later years, she was called “Mother Valve” by her workers for her relentless drive. Eyewitnesses recall her shouting over the roar of pumps:

“They think control is power! But control only keeps the flow steady!”

Myth and Image
After the war, the new Canalist regime elevated her as a folk-technician hero, the embodiment of Bogothian pragmatism and working-class virtue.

Propaganda posters (1950s): Lira in blue overalls, wrench raised, a canal lock behind her, captioned “Strength Is Precision.”

School textbooks: Children learned “The Parable of the Broken Gear,” where Lira repairs a canal gate while lecturing officials on ethics.

Sculpture (1957): The Iron Mother, a bronze statue at Velehrad’s western lock—her eyes fixed on the waterline, hands perpetually stained.

Yet she never joined the party. Interviews late in life show a quiet bitterness:

“They made me an emblem because they couldn’t make me obedient.”

Personality and Legacy
Temperament: Fierce, unsentimental, protective to the point of tyranny.

Politics: Practical socialist; despised slogans, believed in systems.

Faith: None formal, but she referred to the canals as “the only covenant that holds.”

She outlived her son by fourteen years and died in 1959 in her home workshop, surrounded by apprentices. Her tools were sealed in glass at the National Hydrological Museum beside the note she kept on her bench:

“Remember: water forgives nothing, but carries everything.”

The Iron Mother and the Flow
A Bogothian “Science-Historical” Epic of 1943

Author (credited): Radovan Lys, a Ministry writer who was almost certainly the pen name for a collective of propagandists, hydrologists, and one known poet of the rationalist school.
Uncredited technical consultant: a woman believed to be based on Lira Këlaj-Vekir herself.

Structure and Style
Form: A prose epic in twelve sections, written in a hybrid of realist narrative and speculative allegory.

Setting: A semi-futuristic “Hydraulic Republic,” recognizable as Bogothia transposed a century forward—its canals gleaming, its people organized by “flow codes.”

Genre: Wartime “science-historical realism” — the state’s sanctioned term for fiction that reimagined the nation’s rationalist ideals as tools of liberation.

Lira becomes “Matra Lirene,” the archetypal mechanic-scientist who designs a self-repairing canal system that can “think in gradients.” Her son, Aram, is reimagined as “The Diver of the Sun,” a revolutionary engineer who sacrifices himself to prevent the canals from being reversed by invading “storm empires.”

The text alternates between hard, technical prose (blueprint descriptions, pressure tables) and soaring rhetoric about duty, unity, and the ethics of motion. Its motto, repeated like a prayer:

“Flow is freedom; stagnation is sin.”

Ideological Tone
Soviet-Leaning Influence: It borrows imagery from socialist realism—workers as heroes, machinery as moral order—but replaces class struggle with hydraulic ethics.

Arian Reframing: The “sun” is reinterpreted as a symbol of communal illumination, not divine hierarchy, making it palatable to secular and religious readers alike.

Anti-Fascist Undercurrent: The villains, “the Stagnants,” are never named Germans but described as those who “demanded obedience from the rivers.”

The book’s preface explicitly thanks “the engineers of all nations resisting tyranny through repair.”

Reception and Impact
Cultural Phenomenon: Distributed to every canal district, read aloud in workshops and shelters. It becomes both manual and myth.

Propaganda Success: Foreign observers later called it “the most elegant piece of state propaganda ever written in Europe.”

Moral Paradox: Its popularity helps the regime justify its wartime neutrality—“We are fighting the war of repair.”

Science Fiction Elements
For a 1943 novel, it’s remarkably advanced:

Describes autonomous locks that “listen to pressure differentials.”

Foresees computerized water control decades before such systems existed.

Imagines a network of “memory valves” storing data in liquid states—an eerie foreshadowing of cybernetic thinking.

Later Legacy
After the war, it becomes a touchstone of Bogothian paracommunism:

The 1958 “Canalist Education Code” makes excerpts required reading in moral engineering courses.

Feminists of the 1970s reclaim Matra Lirene as the archetype of “mechanical motherhood.”

By the late 20th century, it’s reinterpreted as proto–eco-fiction, seen as a vision of balance between technology and nature.

“Matra Lirene bent over the canal gate, and the water beneath her mirrored not her face, but the future she had repaired.”
— The Iron Mother and the Flow, Chapter XII

Ah—this is the heart of it.
To be Bogothian, in this late-1970s “frozen-flow” era, is to inhabit the contradiction between precision and decay.
The people are neither tragic nor triumphant. They are maintainers of a system that no longer needs them, and yet, somehow, they love it.

1. The National Character: Polite Stoicism
Bogothians are famous for their calm. They do not rush, they do not improvise, and they do not waste.
Patience isn’t a virtue—it’s infrastructure.
Every act, from tightening a valve to signing a form, is a reaffirmation of Flow, the old moral physics that shaped their civilization.
They move through the world like engineers of fate: modest, precise, slightly melancholy.

Foreigners find them unnervingly serene. “They behave,” one Western reporter wrote in 1976, “as though entropy were a civic duty.”

2. Class and Self-Image
There are no aristocrats in the traditional sense, no visible plutocracy. Instead there’s a hierarchy of competence:

Canalkeepers — the engineers, hydrologists, and inspectors who literally keep the country circulating.

Archivists — bureaucrats and scholars who remember the regulations, the stories, and the flows.

Mechanics — the hands and eyes of the system, the quiet heroes.
Every child grows up expecting to maintain something, not to own or command.

The national joke runs:

“We are all middle class, because the upper and lower have both been filed smooth.”

3. Religion and Meaning
Faith survives as bureaucracy. The Arian Church long ago shed theology for ethics.
Its sermons concern maintenance schedules, its hymns quote water levels, and its saints are remembered as reformers of valves.
There is no Heaven—only Equilibrium.

Yet below this polite rationalism, old folk superstitions run like cold groundwater.
People hang charms in the shapes of Glagolitic letters, whisper prayers to canal spirits, and still call vampires unregistered circulations.
It’s all folded neatly into the system—superstition as folklore, not blasphemy.

They speak Liutisk, a Slavo-Gothic language with a soft, murmuring cadence; official documents use the Rond script, indecipherable to outsiders.
To be Bogothian is to live surrounded by unreadable beauty—every sign, form, and letter a secret geometry.
Speech is measured; irony is subtle.
Their humor tends toward maintenance puns and absurd deadpan:

“Nothing lasts forever, except the Temporary Permit.”

Low hills, forested ridges, then a sudden town of yellow stone beside a lock gate.
Trains hiss past wet platforms. The air smells of oil, river silt, and yeast.
At dusk, everything glows with the sodium-orange sheen of industry at rest.

Life is comfortable but constrained: guaranteed housing, modest wages, endless paperwork.
Most evenings end the same way—radio humming, kettle steaming, a copy of Flow and Morality beside the ashtray.

6. Attitudes Toward the World
Bogothians are incurably courteous to foreigners and secretly dismissive of them.
They see capitalist and communist alike as “unbalanced systems.”
Their neutrality isn’t ideology—it’s hydrology. They don’t take sides; they control the sluice gates.
When global crises arise, they neither intervene nor panic; they observe.
And this becomes their defining flaw: wisdom turned into paralysis.

7. Emotional Texture
To be Bogothian is to live in a low, continuous nostalgia—not for the past, but for the continuity of the past.
There is pride, but quiet pride. A sense that one’s hands belong to a chain of maintenance stretching back to Theoderic’s fleeing kin.
Love tends to be reserved; friendship, fierce and loyal.
When Bogothians cry, they do so alone, at a canal’s edge, where the water will “carry the sentiment forward.”

8. The Noir Undercurrent
Behind all this gentility is fatigue.
The vampire scares of the previous decade left psychological residue: a nation that half-believes the dead still walk among them—not monsters, but over-functionaries, people who forgot to stop working.
Every citizen fears becoming one.

So what’s it like to be Bogothian?
It’s like living inside an antique machine that still works perfectly, though nobody remembers why.
You wake to the hiss of steam and the smell of iron, sign your forms in a language no one else can read, and believe—quietly, sincerely—that by keeping everything in order, you are keeping the world from falling apart.

ChatGPT said:
During the Great Wars, Kutna Hora’s Sedlec Ossuary of Balance became more than a macabre curiosity — it became a national symbol of endurance and mortality. Its expansion was both bureaucratic and spiritual, a rare moment when Bogothian rationalism bent under the pressure of death on an industrial scale.

1. 1916–1920: The War Years
By 1916, returning transports from the Eastern Front brought tens of thousands of Bogothian and allied dead.
The ossuary, already famed for its geometric bone chandeliers and wall rosettes, began receiving “unregistered remains” — soldiers who could not be identified or properly buried elsewhere.

To manage the influx, the Ministry of Public Equilibrium authorized the creation of the Great Courtyard, a cloistered square around the original chapel.
At its center rose the Bone Fountain: a circular basin of pale limestone rimmed with femurs and vertebrae set in spirals, designed by architect Jurek Varnský, himself a former canal engineer.
Water from the nearby flow lock cycles continuously through the fountain — a literal circulation of death and purification.

Inscribed in Liutisk-Rond script along the rim:

“So long as the flow continues, none are forgotten.”

The courtyard served as a mourning ground for both sides of the war. Visitors in the 1920s described a stillness “so perfect that even grief felt regulated.”

2. 1939–1945: The Second Expansion
During the Second World War, Sedlec again overflowed.
Refugees, resistance fighters, and civilian victims of bombings were quietly brought here under “Administrative Category 9: Material Remains.”
The state, terrified of contagion and chaos, authorized the ossuary to absorb them into its bureaucratic sanctity.

The Bone Fountain was expanded into a shallow canal basin, its flow linked to the Hradišt water network.
Around it grew the Colonnade of Silence, an open gallery of whitewashed columns filled with niches—each marked not by name but by flow code.
In the candlelight, the codes flickered like constellations.

Many of the bones from this era are not visibly displayed. They are sealed in hexagonal concrete cells beneath the paving, the only marker a small brass valve—the “vent of memory.”

3. Postwar Era
By 1950, the Sedlec Ossuary of Balance covered nearly two hectares, making it the largest single necropolis of its kind in Europe.
Officially, it was categorized as a National Archive of Mortality.
Schoolchildren visited as part of their civic education; inspectors checked the pumps weekly; the water that ran through the Bone Fountain was tested for purity like any other municipal flow.

For Bogothians, this was not horror. It was hygiene.
Death, like water, had to be kept in motion.

4. Symbolism
To outsiders, the sight of the Bone Fountain — vertebrae gleaming beneath a slow whirl of water — seemed nightmarish.
But to Bogothians, it was reassuring: a mechanism for grief that worked, predictably, year after year.

Old women still leave folded maintenance receipts at its base. Newlyweds toss in brass washers instead of coins.

Locals say that when the pumps stop, the dead will finally rest —
but the pumps never stop.

1. The Great Expansion (1960s–1970s)
The ossuary’s outer courtyard was paved in white travertine, with channels that carry a continuous sheet of water between terraces.

The Bone Fountain became the centerpiece of a vast atrium: the skull column expanded into a fluted obelisk of calcified vertebrae and marble, through which water still pulses and seeps, glistening like veins.

Pumps beneath the floor circulate both canal water and filtered rainwater from the roofs — “the continuous cleansing of the past.”

Visitors describe entering through a mist of atomized droplets, hearing the hum of the turbines below, and feeling the cool air laced with lime and salt. It smells faintly of stone, copper, and sanctity.

2. The Tomb of the Unknown
The government added a crypt of anonymity beneath the fountain: ten vaults of ossified chambers representing the “Unrecorded of All Wars.”
Each vault contains sealed white canisters of bone dust, labeled only with coordinates of origin and a small brass valve — the symbolic “breathing port” for the soul.

Ceremonies here are precise, mechanical, and eerily moving:

At each annual remembrance, a canalworker in full gear turns the valve exactly one rotation, releasing a jet of air through the fountain’s core.

Architecturally, the memorial borrows from both the Dresden Zwinger and the Cistercian hydrological cloisters.
High arcades of bleached limestone surround a basin floor where bones and alabaster merge in relief — not piled, but engineered.
Water threads through them in mathematically perfect rivulets.
When sunlight hits, the whole structure glows like mother-of-pearl.

At night, lights within the channels make the water seem to bleed upward.

4. Modern Ritual Life
The Flow of the Dead (annual): citizens release small paper boats carrying garlic and wax across the memorial’s canals.

Inspection Day: the Ministry of Equilibrium performs a televised audit, checking the pressure readings of the fountain; if the numbers are “in balance,” it is said the dead approve of the living.

Student Pilgrimages: Liutisk-language students and calligraphers leave folded sheets inscribed with Rond letters as offerings — symbols of names long erased.

5. The National Mood
By now, the Sedlec Ossuary is the pilgrimage site for Bogothians, regardless of faith. It embodies their paradox: absolute rationalism fused with a tenderness for the dead that borders on superstition.
Foreigners call it “macabre.”
Locals call it “clean.”

To stand before the Zwinger of Bones is to face the heart of Bogothia:
a society that engineered mortality until even grief had a maintenance schedule.

Circuit: only ceremonial loops (no potable mains). Fish passes are closed; freshwater buffers protect intakes.

Exactly — the post-Red-Flow bleach flush is one of those open secrets everyone pretends not to know about but smells anyway.

Officially, the Ministry of Equilibrium describes it as the “white phase of the purification cycle.” Unofficially, it’s just bleach, or more precisely, a stabilized hypochlorite-lime solution used to stop the limestone and bone from taking on a permanent pink hue.

The Bleach Flush (White Phase)
Timing:
Begins at midnight on the final day of the Red Flow. The pumps reverse briefly to drain the tinted wine water, and by dawn, the sluices hiss with a faint chlorine scent. Locals say “the dead are brushing their teeth.”

Chemistry:

3 % sodium hypochlorite with crushed limestone buffer to keep the pH gentle on calcium phosphate.

A small dose of hydrogen peroxide for “optical brightening.”

Monitored by the Office of Calcic Preservation, whose inspectors wear bone-white oilskins and brass respirators.

Procedure:

Valves marked with the white rond (a small circle with a dot) are opened.

The canals run clear for one hour, then the solution enters at low pressure.

Fountains are allowed to foam lightly—“the cleansing breath.”

After twelve hours, pure canal water follows, neutralizing and resealing the stone.

Sensory effect:
The whole city smells faintly like a swimming pool and wet limestone. Tourists wrinkle their noses; locals find it reassuring. The bones gleam a startling, almost porcelain white in the morning sun.

Folklore:
Old canalworkers insist that the bleach keeps not only stains away but also spirits contained—that red residue invites “the thirsty dead.” In rural superstition, it’s said the ghosts cling to color; the city must turn itself white again to stay safe.

Aesthetic paradox:
Bogothians celebrate the Red Flow for its beauty but pride themselves on the immaculate aftermath. Newspapers run side-by-side photos: Ruda-tȟek on one page, Bleda-tȟek (“white run”) on the next. Children know both rhymes by heart.

The bones and lime don’t just stay inside the memorial — over decades, they’ve leached into the entire hydrological system.

1. The Canal Chemistry
Ever since the ossuary’s expansion in the 1950s, the Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ concentrations in the downstream canals have been well above natural equilibrium.
Official records euphemistically describe the phenomenon as “calcic enrichment.”

Typical readings from the Velehrad Hydrological Survey (1974):

Calcium hardness: 480–520 mg/L (vs 150 mg/L in upstream controls)

Phosphate levels: 2.5–3.0 mg/L (vs 0.2 mg/L baseline)

pH: stable 7.9–8.2 — held there intentionally to prevent bone dissolution spikes.

The water looks pristine — almost too clear — with a faint bluish haze that photographers love. But if you dip your fingers in, it feels chalky, as if the nation’s past were still in suspension.

2. Ecological Consequences
“Bonewater bloom.” The phosphate feeds a delicate biolayer of pearly algae that clings to canal walls and slow-moving sluices. Locals call it mlečna koža (“milk skin”). It glows faintly in ultraviolet light, giving the night canals their eerie shimmer.

Calciferous fauna. Snails, mussels, and crustaceans have developed thicker shells and an almost ceramic texture. Taxonomists jokingly classify them under Classis ossiphila, “bone-lovers.”

Clogging risk. Engineers must scrape scale from turbine fins weekly; some plants now have dedicated descaling brigades. The residue is carted to cement works — “recycling holiness into masonry.”

3. Human & Industrial Impact
Tap water: perfectly safe by official measure, but tastes “like wet plaster.” Locals claim it “makes the bones strong.”

Laundry: clothes come out stiff if washed without additives; detergent companies advertise “softeners for sacred water.”

Concrete: mixes beautifully. Bogothian cement, rich in natural phosphate, sets harder and smoother than any imported kind. The Ministry calls it hydraulic virtue.

4. Cultural Resonance
The population quietly believes the canal system is now mineralized with ancestry.
They joke that the canals have “a skeleton of their own.”

Folk songs reinterpreted in the 1960s call the main waterways “white veins of the land.”
There’s even a saying among the canalkeepers:

“To drink the flow is to borrow the bones of your fathers.”

5. Modern Complications
By the late 1970s, international inspectors begin calling it chronic supersaturation — warning that long-term deposition could turn lower channels into concrete troughs.
Bogothia’s response is characteristically bureaucratic: the Canal Calcification Commission (CCC), founded 1978, which issues elaborate color-coded reports confirming that “structural whiteness remains within acceptable tolerance.”

Privately, every hydrologist knows:
The nation’s entire water system is becoming one vast ossuary.

Ah yes — “The White Canals of Bohgothia” (Liutisk: Bledne Kanali Bogothii) — the national earworm that everyone thought was patriotic, but which, on closer inspection, was practically a hymn of bureaucratic despair.

It debuted in 1932, composed by Marko Hrubec (lyrics) and Ivana Drotár (music), both employees of the Ministry of Equilibrium’s cultural bureau — which was precisely why no one noticed what they were really saying.

🎵 Surface Meaning
On the surface, it’s a sentimental waltz about national pride:

“White run the canals through our hills and our homes,
they shine like our fathers, they flow like our bones…”

It sounded like a technocratic lullaby — reassuring, clean, civic.
The phrase “white canals” invoked the post-Red-Flow purification ritual, the country’s trademark devotion to clarity, balance, and continuity.

💀 The Irony Beneath
But the deeper verses (the ones rarely broadcast on radio after 1935) reveal the irony — a quiet, bureaucratic nihilism.

“We wash and we wash till no color remains,
the stains we can’t name still return in the drains.”

“Our children drink whiteness, our elders the same,
and the dead whisper softly the valve numbers’ name.”

It’s not patriotic at all. It’s a portrait of a people so obsessed with purity — both literal and moral — that they’ve bleached their own soul out of existence.
The “white canals” aren’t symbols of glory; they’re arteries calcified by control.

🧂 Cultural Context
When first performed in Praga’s Riverside Pavilion, it was introduced as a “hydrological romance.”

Within a month, it was being hummed by street cleaners and canal inspectors — the very people trapped inside the system it mocked.

The refrain “Flow white, flow right” (Liutisk: “Tȟek bledne, tȟek prave”) became an official slogan for the 1933 municipal purity campaign.

No one noticed that in Liutisk, tȟek prave can also mean “flow obediently.”

🪶 Legacy
After World War II, it was revived as a nostalgic anthem;

by the 1960s, underground poets quoted it ironically, to suggest the futility of reform;

by the 1970s, it was played without irony again, at canalkeeper retirement banquets.

Bogothia’s full circle — institutional melancholy mistaken for virtue.

🎶 Bledne Kanali Bogothii
(The White Canals of Bohgothia)
Words: Marko Hrubec
Music: Ivana Drotár
(First performed, Praga, 1932 — Banned verse restored from 1936 samizdat edition)

I.
Liutisk (Rond orthography):

Bledne kanali, pod sveťom spet,
teče v nadu, tiche, čiste, svet.
Bledne kanali, naš dom i krov,
sveti tȟek — to Bohgothijov hrov.

English translation:

White run the canals beneath the light,
flowing upward, silent, clean, and bright.
White run the canals through hearth and home,
holy flow — the tomb of Bohgothia’s own.

(Note: “to Bohgothijov hrov” literally means “our grave,” not “our nation.” The double meaning was likely intentional.)

II.
Liutisk:

Perem i perem, bez krve, bez ran,
no v drenazah čujes — šepot stari lan.
Perem i perem, dok’ svet’nost ne tȟek,
ostav’ nas bledne, ostav’ nas mek.

English:

We wash and we wash, no blood, no pain,
yet in the drains you can hear old chains.
We wash and we wash till the whiteness runs weak,
leave us pale, leave us meek.

(This verse was reportedly “edited for tone” in the 1934 reprint; the phrase “old chains” was deemed subversive.)

III. (Banned Verse — 1935)
Liutisk:

Pod ventilom spiše, dušon tȟek prave,
ne v vodi, v nadu, spominki stave.
Čis’ta je zemja, no mrtvejši svet,
bledne kanali — narodov greh.

English:

Beneath the valves they sleep, their souls flow right,
not in water, but in pressure’s might.
The land is clean, but the world is dead,
white canals — the nation’s dread.

(Suppressed by the Ministry for “fatalistic implications inconsistent with hydrological optimism.”)

IV. (Final Chorus)
Liutisk:

Bledne kanali, tečete z nas,
dok’ nebo vrati posledni glas.
Bledne kanali, naša krov, naš kost,
Bohgothia bela, Bohgothia most.

English:

White canals, you flow from our veins,
till heaven returns the final strains.
White canals, our roof, our bone,
Bohgothia white, Bohgothia alone.

(The word “most” here means both “bridge” and “solitude.”)

Musical Notes:
3/4 tempo waltz, andante sostenuto.

Often performed by municipal canal bands using brass, celesta, and water harmonica.

The refrain “Bledne kanali, naša krov, naš kost” became the tag-line of a state poster campaign in 1934: “Clean Water, Clean Nation.”

Later Interpretations
1950s version: arranged for children’s choirs, omitting the second and third verses entirely.

1970s noir revival: performed by singer Toma Želen, slowed to half tempo with electric harmonium — transformed into a dirge for a nation bleached of color and memory.

Modern (post-2000) art installations: projected onto canal walls in Liutisk-Gothic script, with actual canalwater running across the light.

🌀 I. The Three Waves of Slavicization
1️⃣ Contact Phonology (6th–9th c.) — Bohemian substrate
The first Slavic settlers’ speech is full of palatalization and fronted vowels.

/k g x s z/ → [ c ʒ ɕ ʑ ] before /i e j/

2️⃣ Prosodic & Vocalic Drift (10th–13th c.) — Slavic dominance in towns
Gothic’s long/short vowels lose quantitative value and gain qualitative contrast:

Proto-Gothic	Early Bogothic	Liutisk IPA	Example
ī	í > i / ji	[i ~ ji]	stilan → stjit ‘to steal’
ai	ej / ie	[e ~ je]	bai → bej

3️⃣ Epenthesis & Cluster Simplification (15th–18th c.) — Phonotactic balance
Slavic speakers dislike Gothic’s heavy consonant clusters:

wrst > vrest > verest

brōþr > broter > brodar

Conversely, Gothic speakers reintroduce prothetic vowels before liquid initials, producing a specifically Bogothian sound:

runa → aruna, ljus → iljus.

This gives the modern pattern of alternating “open syllable” structure, typical of West Slavic phonotactics.

🔠 II. Final Liutisk Phoneme Inventory (c. 1900)
Stops	Fricatives	Nasals	Liquids	Glides
p b t d k g	f v s z ʃ ʒ x	m n ɲ	r rʲ l lʲ	j w
Vowels: /i ɪ e ɛ a ɔ o u ə/ (+ fronted ɪ/ɛ after soft consonants)

Phonological Rules (summarized)

Palatal harmony: hard consonant + front vowel → soft allophone.

Word-initial voicing assimilation: zg > sk, sv > sf.

Final devoicing: brad > brat (word-final).

Stress: primary on root; enclitic secondary may appear two syllables later.

🧩 III. Orthographic Reflections
Palatalization indicated by Glagolitic diacritics: Ⰸ → Ⱌ = [kʲ]; Ⱄ → Ⱎ = [sʲ].

Roman transliteration marks softness with an acute accent: ć, ś, ĺ, ń.

The ancient Gothic þ survives only in ecclesiastical liturgy ( ⱅ = /θ/ ), but common speech replaced it centuries earlier.

🧠 In-World Consequences
Spoken Liutisk sounds simultaneously familiar and foreign to a Slavic ear—like a Czech speaker reading Icelandic.

The educated classes keep some “hard” Gothic pronunciations as prestige variants (analogous to English RP).
